report:
**Conclusion:** Hypnosis may help some individuals feel more motivated or manage cravings, but it is **not proven to improve long-term smoking cessation reliably**. The strongest synthesis of the evidence—a 2019 Cochrane review of randomized trials with at least six months’ follow-up—found insufficient, low-certainty evidence to conclude that hypnotherapy works better than no treatment or established behavioral treatments. The studies were generally small and variable in how hypnosis was delivered.

Therefore, hypnosis can be a personal adjunct if someone finds it appealing and it does not replace evidence-based care, but it should not be relied on as the primary quit method. Proven options include behavioral counseling plus medication (e.g., nicotine-replacement therapy, varenicline, or bupropion where medically appropriate); combining counseling and medication is commonly recommended.

Discuss medication suitability and a quit plan with a clinician, especially during pregnancy or with mental-health conditions, seizure history, or relevant medicines.

- Cochrane Review: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001008_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking

- NICE tobacco prevention and cessation guideline: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209
